# cpubits/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![no_std]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)#![doc = include_str!("../README.md")]
[3](https://docs.rs#3)#![doc(
[4](https://docs.rs#4)    html_logo_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RustCrypto/media/6ee8e381/logo.svg",
[5](https://docs.rs#5)    html_favicon_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RustCrypto/media/6ee8e381/logo.svg"
[6](https://docs.rs#6))]
[7](https://docs.rs#7)#![warn(clippy::pedantic)]
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! # Supported bit sizes
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! This crate supports the following bit sizes:
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! - `16`
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! - `32`
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! - `64`
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! This matches the available options for `target_pointer_width` in `rustc`:
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! ```text
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! expected values for `target_pointer_width` are: `16`, `32`, and `64`
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! ```
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! # Overriding the selection result via `cfg`
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! This crate supports overriding its detection heuristics via an explicit `cfg` setting:
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! - `cpubits = "16"`: force 16-bit
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! - `cpubits = "32"`: force 32-bit
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! - `cpubits = "64"`: force 64-bit
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! This can be useful for testing different backends, and also in the event you would like to
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! override the default detection result (in which case we would appreciate it if you opened an
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! issue and let us know why).
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! You can set `cfg` via the `RUSTFLAGS` environment variable:
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! ```console
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! $ RUSTFLAGS='--cfg cpubits="64"' cargo build --release
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! ```
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! Or you can persistently configure it for your project in `.cargo/config.toml`:
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! ```toml
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! # In .cargo/config.toml
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! [build]
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! rustflags = ['--cfg', 'cpubits="64"']
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! ```
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! ## Lint configuration for `cfg(cpubits)`
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! If you are using the `cpubits!` macro you will notice the following warning being emitted:
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! ```text
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! warning: unexpected `cfg` condition name: `cpubits`
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! ```
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! You will need to add the following configuration to your `Cargo.toml` to silence the warning:
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! ```toml
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! [lints.rust.unexpected_cfgs]
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! level = "warn"
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! check-cfg = ['cfg(cpubits, values("16", "32", "64"))']
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)
[64](https://docs.rs#64)// End of toplevel rustdoc, beginning of macro documentation. We put the detailed docs on the macro
[65](https://docs.rs#65)// itself so we can re-export it, and people can easily get to these docs from the re-exported
[66](https://docs.rs#66)// version.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// A macro for defining code based on the optimal word size to use for the target, as chosen
[69](https://docs.rs#69)/// heuristically at compile-time using `cfg`-based predicates.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)///
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// # Usage
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///
[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// The macro works like a `match` expression that takes an implicit argument representing the
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// number of CPU bits, which is one of `16`, `32`, or `64`.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)///
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// Use this macro to conditionally emit code specific to certain CPU word sizes, e.g. defining
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// types at compile-time based on the word size.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)///
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// The macro doesn't create a new block and supports arbitrary statements in toplevel code, just
[80](https://docs.rs#80)/// like the `cfg-if` crate (whose guts it recycles).
[81](https://docs.rs#81)///
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// ## Basic usage
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// ```
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// cpubits::cpubits! {
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///     16 => { pub type Word = u16; }
[87](https://docs.rs#87)///     32 => { pub type Word = u32; }
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///     64 => { pub type Word = u64; }
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// }
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// ```
[91](https://docs.rs#91)///
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// NOTE: rustc will complain: "warning: unexpected `cfg` condition name: `cpubits`"
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// See the [lint configuration for `cfg(cpubits)`](./index.html#lint-configuration-for-cfgcpubits)
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// documentation for how to silence the warning.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)///
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// ## Grouping multiple bit sizes
[98](https://docs.rs#98)///
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// If you would like to group together 16-bit and 32-bit platforms, you can do so as follows:
[100](https://docs.rs#100)///
[101](https://docs.rs#101)/// ```
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// cpubits::cpubits! {
[103](https://docs.rs#103)///     16 | 32 => { pub type Word = u32; }
[104](https://docs.rs#104)///     64      => { pub type Word = u64; }
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// }
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// ```
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// ## Handling single-size cases
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// If you only want a block to run for a specific size, e.g. to know when it's possible to write
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// `impl From<u64> for MyWordNewtype`, you can do the following:
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// ```
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// # type Word = u64;
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// pub struct MyWordNewtype(Word);
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// cpubits::cpubits! {
[118](https://docs.rs#118)///     64 => {
[119](https://docs.rs#119)///         impl From<u64> for MyWordNewtype {
[120](https://docs.rs#120)///             #[inline]
[121](https://docs.rs#121)///             fn from(n: u64) -> MyWordNewtype {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///                 MyWordNewtype(n)
[123](https://docs.rs#123)///             }
[124](https://docs.rs#124)///         }
[125](https://docs.rs#125)///     }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// }
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// ```
[128](https://docs.rs#128)///
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// ## Use as an expression
[130](https://docs.rs#130)///
[131](https://docs.rs#131)/// It's also possible to use the macro as an expression, although in somewhat limited contexts
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// due to its attribute handling:
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// ```
[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// fn detected_cpubits() -> u32 {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///     cpubits::cpubits! {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///         16 => { 16 }
[138](https://docs.rs#138)///         32 => { 32 }
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///         64 => { 64 }
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///     }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// }
[142](https://docs.rs#142)/// ```
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// # Selection rules
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// The macro augments `target_pointer_width`-based selection with specific overrides which promote
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// certain targets from 32-bit to 64-bit ones.
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// This 64-bit promotion occurs if `any` of the following `cfg`s are true:
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// - `armv7`: `all(target_arch = "arm", target_feature = "v7")`
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// - `wasm32`: `target_arch = "wasm32"`
[152](https://docs.rs#152)#[macro_export]
[153](https://docs.rs#153)macro_rules! cpubits {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    // Only run the given block if we have selected a 16-bit word size, i.e. the code will be
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    // ignored on 32-bit and 64-bit platforms.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    ( 16 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        $crate::cpubits! {
[158](https://docs.rs#158)            16 => { $( $tokens )* },
[159](https://docs.rs#159)            32 | 64 => { }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    };
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    // Only run the given block if we have selected a 32-bit word size, i.e. the code will be
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    // ignored on 32-bit and 64-bit platforms.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    ( 32 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        $crate::cpubits! {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            16 => { }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            32 => { $( $tokens )* }
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            64 => { }
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    };
[172](https://docs.rs#172)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    // Only run the given block if we have selected a 64-bit word size, i.e. the code will be
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    // ignored on 16-bit and 32-bit platforms.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    ( 64 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        $crate::cpubits! {
[177](https://docs.rs#177)            16 | 32 => { }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            64 => { $( $tokens )* }
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    };
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    // Only run the block on 16-bit and 32-bit targets.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    ( 16 | 32 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)        $crate::cpubits! {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)            16 => { $( $tokens )* }
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            32 => { $( $tokens )* }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            64 => { }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    };
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    // Only run the block on 32-bit and 64-bit targets.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    ( 32 | 64 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        $crate::cpubits! {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            16 => { }
[195](https://docs.rs#195)            32 => { $( $tokens )* }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)            64 => { $( $tokens )* }
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        }
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    };
[199](https://docs.rs#199)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    // Select between 16-bit and 32-bit options, where no code will be generated for 64-bit targets
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    (
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
[203](https://docs.rs#203)        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    ) => {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        $crate::cpubits! {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            16 => { $( $tokens16 )* }
[207](https://docs.rs#207)            32 => { $( $tokens32 )* }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)            64 => { }
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        }
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    };
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    // Select between 32-bit and 64-bit options, where no code will be generated for 16-bit targets
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    (
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    ) => {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        $crate::cpubits! {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)            16 => { }
[219](https://docs.rs#219)            32 => { $( $tokens32 )* }
[220](https://docs.rs#220)            64 => { $( $tokens64 )* }
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        }
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    };
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    // Select between 16-bit and 32-bit options, where 64-bit will use the 32-bit option
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    (
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        32 | 64 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    ) => {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        $crate::cpubits! {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)            16 => { $( $tokens16 )* }
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            32 => { $( $tokens32 )* }
[232](https://docs.rs#232)            64 => { $( $tokens32 )* }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)        }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    };
[235](https://docs.rs#235)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    // Select between 32-bit and 64-bit options, where 16-bit will use the 32-bit option
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    (
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        16 | 32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    ) => {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        $crate::cpubits! {
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            16 => { $( $tokens32 )* }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)            32 => { $( $tokens32 )* }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)            64 => { $( $tokens64 )* }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    };
[247](https://docs.rs#247)
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    // The general API which runs a different block for each possible word size
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    (
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    ) => {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        $crate::cpubits! {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)            // `cfg` selector for 64-bit target overrides
[256](https://docs.rs#256)            #[cfg(enable_64_bit = any(
[257](https://docs.rs#257)                // ARMv7
[258](https://docs.rs#258)                all(target_arch = "arm", target_feature = "v7"),
[259](https://docs.rs#259)                // WASM
[260](https://docs.rs#260)                target_arch = "wasm32",
[261](https://docs.rs#261)            ))]
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            16 => { $( $tokens16 )* }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            32 => { $( $tokens32 )* }
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            64 => { $( $tokens64 )* }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    };
[267](https://docs.rs#267)
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    // Same API as immediately above, but with a pseudo-attribute we use to pass the `cfg` overrides
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    // for `target_pointer_width` that promote a 32-bit target into a 64-bit one.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    (
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        #[cfg(enable_64_bit = $($enable_64_bit:tt)+ )]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
[274](https://docs.rs#274)        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ) => {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        $crate::cfg_if! {
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            @__items () ;
[278](https://docs.rs#278)            // The following are effectively `if`/`else` clauses in a Lispy syntax, where each
[279](https://docs.rs#279)            // 2-tuple is `( ( predicate ) ( body ) )`. The first clause with a matching predicate
[280](https://docs.rs#280)            // is taken and its body executed and the rest are ignored just like `if`/`else`.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)            //
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            // We first match on each of the explicit overrides, and if none of them are configured
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            // apply our heuristic logic which allows certain targets to be overridden to use
[284](https://docs.rs#284)            // 64-bit backends, as configured in the `enable_64_bit` predicate above.
[285](https://docs.rs#285)            (
[286](https://docs.rs#286)                ( cpubits = "16" )
[287](https://docs.rs#287)                ( $( $tokens16 )* )
[288](https://docs.rs#288)            ),
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            (
[290](https://docs.rs#290)                ( cpubits = "32" )
[291](https://docs.rs#291)                ( $( $tokens32 )* )
[292](https://docs.rs#292)            ),
[293](https://docs.rs#293)            (
[294](https://docs.rs#294)                ( cpubits = "64" )
[295](https://docs.rs#295)                ( $( $tokens64 )* )
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            ),
[297](https://docs.rs#297)            (
[298](https://docs.rs#298)                ( target_pointer_width = "16" )
[299](https://docs.rs#299)                ( $( $tokens16 )* )
[300](https://docs.rs#300)            ),
[301](https://docs.rs#301)            (
[302](https://docs.rs#302)                ( all(target_pointer_width = "32", not($( $enable_64_bit )+)) )
[303](https://docs.rs#303)                ( $( $tokens32 )* )
[304](https://docs.rs#304)            ),
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            (
[306](https://docs.rs#306)                ( any(target_pointer_width = "64", $( $enable_64_bit )+) )
[307](https://docs.rs#307)                ( $( $tokens64 )* )
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            ),
[309](https://docs.rs#309)            (
[310](https://docs.rs#310)                ()
[311](https://docs.rs#311)                ( compile_error!("unsupported target pointer width") )
[312](https://docs.rs#312)            ),
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        }
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    };
[315](https://docs.rs#315)}
[316](https://docs.rs#316)
[317](https://docs.rs#317)/// Vendored copy of the `cfg_if::cfg_if` macro.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)/// Copyright (c) 2014 Alex Crichton. Dual-licensed Apache 2.0 + MIT.
[319](https://docs.rs#319)///
[320](https://docs.rs#320)/// NOTE: though this is marked `doc(hidden)`, it is considered a stable part of the public API.
[321](https://docs.rs#321)#[doc(hidden)]
[322](https://docs.rs#322)#[macro_export]
[323](https://docs.rs#323)macro_rules! cfg_if {
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    // NOTE(cpubits): we deliberately include the original frontend even though we don't use it
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    // internally within this crate so consumers of `cpubits` can use the vendored `cfg_if` instead
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    // of requiring both `cpubits` and `cfg-if`.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    (
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        if #[cfg( $($i_meta:tt)+ )] { $( $i_tokens:tt )* }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        $(
[330](https://docs.rs#330)            else if #[cfg( $($ei_meta:tt)+ )] { $( $ei_tokens:tt )* }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        )*
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        $(
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            else { $( $e_tokens:tt )* }
[334](https://docs.rs#334)        )?
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    ) => {
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        $crate::cfg_if! {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            @__items () ;
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            (( $($i_meta)+ ) ( $( $i_tokens )* )),
[339](https://docs.rs#339)            $(
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                (( $($ei_meta)+ ) ( $( $ei_tokens )* )),
[341](https://docs.rs#341)            )*
[342](https://docs.rs#342)            $(
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                (() ( $( $e_tokens )* )),
[344](https://docs.rs#344)            )?
[345](https://docs.rs#345)        }
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    };
[347](https://docs.rs#347)
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    // Internal and recursive macro to emit all the items
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    //
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    // Collects all the previous cfgs in a list at the beginning, so they can be
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    // negated. After the semicolon are all the remaining items.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    (@__items ( $( ($($_:tt)*) , )* ) ; ) => {};
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    (
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        @__items ( $( ($($no:tt)+) , )* ) ;
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        (( $( $($yes:tt)+ )? ) ( $( $tokens:tt )* )),
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        $( $rest:tt , )*
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    ) => {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        // Emit all items within one block, applying an appropriate #[cfg]. The
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        // #[cfg] will require all `$yes` matchers specified and must also negate
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        // all previous matchers.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        #[cfg(all(
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            $( $($yes)+ , )?
[363](https://docs.rs#363)            not(any( $( $($no)+ ),* ))
[364](https://docs.rs#364)        ))]
[365](https://docs.rs#365)        // Subtle: You might think we could put `$( $tokens )*` here. But if
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        // that contains multiple items then the `#[cfg(all(..))]` above would
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        // only apply to the first one. By wrapping `$( $tokens )*` in this
[368](https://docs.rs#368)        // macro call, we temporarily group the items into a single thing (the
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        // macro call) that will be included/excluded by the `#[cfg(all(..))]`
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        // as appropriate. If the `#[cfg(all(..))]` succeeds, the macro call
[371](https://docs.rs#371)        // will be included, and then evaluated, producing `$( $tokens )*`. See
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        // also the "issue #90" test below.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        $crate::cfg_if! { @__temp_group $( $tokens )* }
[374](https://docs.rs#374)
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        // Recurse to emit all other items in `$rest`, and when we do so add all
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        // our `$yes` matchers to the list of `$no` matchers as future emissions
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        // will have to negate everything we just matched as well.
[378](https://docs.rs#378)        $crate::cfg_if! {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            @__items ( $( ($($no)+) , )* $( ($($yes)+) , )? ) ;
[380](https://docs.rs#380)            $( $rest , )*
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    };
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    // See the "Subtle" comment above.
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    (@__temp_group $( $tokens:tt )* ) => {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        $( $tokens )*
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    };
[388](https://docs.rs#388)}
[389](https://docs.rs#389)
[390](https://docs.rs#390)/// Constant representing the detection result from `cpubits!` on the current target.
[391](https://docs.rs#391)pub const CPUBITS: u32 = {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    cpubits! {
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        16 => { 16 }
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        32 => { 32 }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)        64 => { 64 }
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    }
[397](https://docs.rs#397)};
[398](https://docs.rs#398)
[399](https://docs.rs#399)#[cfg(test)]
[400](https://docs.rs#400)mod tests {
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    use super::CPUBITS;
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// Return the expected number of bits for the target.
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    #[cfg(not(any(cpubits = "16", cpubits = "32", cpubits = "64")))]
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    fn expected_bits() -> u32 {
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        // Duplicated 64-bit override predicates need to go here
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        if cfg!(any(
[408](https://docs.rs#408)            // ARMv7
[409](https://docs.rs#409)            all(target_arch = "arm", target_feature = "v7"),
[410](https://docs.rs#410)            // WASM
[411](https://docs.rs#411)            target_arch = "wasm32"
[412](https://docs.rs#412)        )) {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)            64
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        } else {
[415](https://docs.rs#415)            usize::BITS
[416](https://docs.rs#416)        }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    }
[418](https://docs.rs#418)
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    #[cfg(not(any(cpubits = "16", cpubits = "32", cpubits = "64")))]
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    #[test]
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    fn cpubits_works() {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        assert_eq!(CPUBITS, expected_bits());
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// Explicit test for ARMv7 so we can see the predicate is working
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    #[cfg(all(target_arch = "arm", target_feature = "v7"))]
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    #[test]
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    fn cpubits_on_armv7_is_64bit() {
[429](https://docs.rs#429)        assert_eq!(CPUBITS, 64);
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    }
[431](https://docs.rs#431)
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// Explicit test for WASM so we can see the predicate is working
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    #[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    #[test]
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    fn cpubits_on_wasm_is_64bit() {
[436](https://docs.rs#436)        assert_eq!(CPUBITS, 64);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    }
[438](https://docs.rs#438)
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// Test for the `16 | 32` syntax.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    #[cfg(not(any(cpubits = "16", cpubits = "32", cpubits = "64")))]
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    #[test]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    fn cpubits_16_or_32_vs_64() {
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        const BITS: u32 = {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)            cpubits! {
[445](https://docs.rs#445)                16 | 32 => { 32 }
[446](https://docs.rs#446)                64 => { 64 }
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            }
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        };
[449](https://docs.rs#449)
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        match expected_bits() {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            16 | 32 => assert_eq!(32, BITS),
[452](https://docs.rs#452)            64 => assert_eq!(64, BITS),
[453](https://docs.rs#453)            bits => unreachable!("#{bits}-bits should be one of: 16, 32, 64"),
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        }
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    }
[456](https://docs.rs#456)
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    #[cfg(cpubits = "32")]
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    #[test]
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    fn cpubits_32_bit_override() {
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        assert_eq!(CPUBITS, 32);
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    }
[462](https://docs.rs#462)}

# cpubits in cpubits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpubits/0.1.1/i686-pc-windows-msvc/cpubits/macro.cpubits.html

```
macro_rules! cpubits {
    ( 16 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 32 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 64 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 16 | 32 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 32 | 64 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    (
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 | 64 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        16 | 32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        #[cfg(enable_64_bit = $($enable_64_bit:tt)+ )]
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

A macro for defining code based on the optimal word size to use for the target, as chosen
heuristically at compile-time using `cfg`-based predicates.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The macro works like a `match` expression that takes an implicit argument representing the
number of CPU bits, which is one of `16`, `32`, or `64`.

Use this macro to conditionally emit code specific to certain CPU word sizes, e.g. defining types at compile-time based on the word size.

The macro doesn’t create a new block and supports arbitrary statements in toplevel code, just
like the `cfg-if` crate (whose guts it recycles).

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage)Basic usage

```
cpubits::cpubits! {
    16 => { pub type Word = u16; }
    32 => { pub type Word = u32; }
    64 => { pub type Word = u64; }
}
```
NOTE: rustc will complain: “warning: unexpected `cfg` condition name: `cpubits`”

See the [lint configuration for  cfg(cpubits)](https://docs.rs/index.html#lint-configuration-for-cfgcpubits)
documentation for how to silence the warning.

[§](https://docs.rs#grouping-multiple-bit-sizes)Grouping multiple bit sizes

If you would like to group together 16-bit and 32-bit platforms, you can do so as follows:

```
cpubits::cpubits! {
    16 | 32 => { pub type Word = u32; }
    64      => { pub type Word = u64; }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#handling-single-size-cases)Handling single-size cases

If you only want a block to run for a specific size, e.g. to know when it’s possible to write
`impl From<u64> for MyWordNewtype`, you can do the following:

```
pub struct MyWordNewtype(Word);
cpubits::cpubits! {
    64 => {
        impl From<u64> for MyWordNewtype {
            #[inline]
            fn from(n: u64) -> MyWordNewtype {
                MyWordNewtype(n)
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#use-as-an-expression)Use as an expression

It’s also possible to use the macro as an expression, although in somewhat limited contexts due to its attribute handling:

```
fn detected_cpubits() -> u32 {
    cpubits::cpubits! {
        16 => { 16 }
        32 => { 32 }
        64 => { 64 }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#selection-rules)Selection rules

The macro augments `target_pointer_width`-based selection with specific overrides which promote
certain targets from 32-bit to 64-bit ones.

This 64-bit promotion occurs if `any` of the following `cfg`s are true:

- `armv7`:- `all(target_arch = "arm", target_feature = "v7")`
- `wasm32`:- `target_arch = "wasm32"`

---

# CPUBITS in cpubits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpubits/0.1.1/i686-pc-windows-msvc/cpubits/constant.CPUBITS.html

`pub const CPUBITS: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html) = { 32 }; // 32u32## Expand description

Constant representing the detection result from `cpubits!` on the current target.

---

        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };

        32 | 64 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }

        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }

# cpubits in cpubits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpubits/latest/target-redirect/cpubits/macro.cpubits.html

```
macro_rules! cpubits {
    ( 16 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 32 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 64 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 16 | 32 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    ( 32 | 64 => { $( $tokens:tt )* } ) => { ... };
    (
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 | 64 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        16 | 32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
    (
        #[cfg(enable_64_bit = $($enable_64_bit:tt)+ )]
        16 => { $( $tokens16:tt )* }
        32 => { $( $tokens32:tt )* }
        64 => { $( $tokens64:tt )* }
    ) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

A macro for defining code based on the optimal word size to use for the target, as chosen
heuristically at compile-time using `cfg`-based predicates.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The macro works like a `match` expression that takes an implicit argument representing the
number of CPU bits, which is one of `16`, `32`, or `64`.

Use this macro to conditionally emit code specific to certain CPU word sizes, e.g. defining types at compile-time based on the word size.

The macro doesn’t create a new block and supports arbitrary statements in toplevel code, just
like the `cfg-if` crate (whose guts it recycles).

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage)Basic usage

```
cpubits::cpubits! {
    16 => { pub type Word = u16; }
    32 => { pub type Word = u32; }
    64 => { pub type Word = u64; }
}
```
NOTE: rustc will complain: “warning: unexpected `cfg` condition name: `cpubits`”

See the [lint configuration for  cfg(cpubits)](https://docs.rs/index.html#lint-configuration-for-cfgcpubits)
documentation for how to silence the warning.

[§](https://docs.rs#grouping-multiple-bit-sizes)Grouping multiple bit sizes

If you would like to group together 16-bit and 32-bit platforms, you can do so as follows:

```
cpubits::cpubits! {
    16 | 32 => { pub type Word = u32; }
    64      => { pub type Word = u64; }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#handling-single-size-cases)Handling single-size cases

If you only want a block to run for a specific size, e.g. to know when it’s possible to write
`impl From<u64> for MyWordNewtype`, you can do the following:

```
pub struct MyWordNewtype(Word);
cpubits::cpubits! {
    64 => {
        impl From<u64> for MyWordNewtype {
            #[inline]
            fn from(n: u64) -> MyWordNewtype {
                MyWordNewtype(n)
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#use-as-an-expression)Use as an expression

It’s also possible to use the macro as an expression, although in somewhat limited contexts due to its attribute handling:

```
fn detected_cpubits() -> u32 {
    cpubits::cpubits! {
        16 => { 16 }
        32 => { 32 }
        64 => { 64 }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#selection-rules)Selection rules

The macro augments `target_pointer_width`-based selection with specific overrides which promote
certain targets from 32-bit to 64-bit ones.

This 64-bit promotion occurs if `any` of the following `cfg`s are true:

- `armv7`:- `all(target_arch = "arm", target_feature = "v7")`
- `wasm32`:- `target_arch = "wasm32"`

# xpile_contract_frontend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-contract-frontend/0.1.615/xpile_contract_frontend/

## Expand description

ContractFrontend trait — proof-lane parsing abstraction.

Parses notation (LaTeX math + theorem environments, Lean 4 theorem
text, mdBook with embedded math) into contract equation YAML.
Sibling of [`xpile_frontend::Frontend`]; the proof lane is disjoint
from the code lane and does NOT produce meta-HIR.

Architectural invariants codified in
`contracts/xpile-contract-frontend-trait-v1.yaml`.

- Result of parsing a notation source into the proof-lane contract
substrate. `equations_only`invariant: NO meta-HIR is produced or mutated by ContractFrontend implementations.
- [Proof](https://docs.rs/struct.ProofObligation.html)- Obligation
- A single proof obligation parsed from a theorem-class environment.

# xpile_ffi_manifest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-ffi-manifest/0.1.615/xpile_ffi_manifest/

## Expand description

FFI boundary registry.

In a hybrid transpile (e.g. Python + C extension, Python + CUDA kernel), the agent must know exactly which symbols cross language lines and what their Rust shim signatures should be. This crate is the single source of truth for that mapping within a session.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FfiEmit](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiEmitError.html)- Error
- PMAT-899 (Sprint-2 Tier 2): a reconciled boundary could not be lowered to a
Rust FFI shim because a recovered parameter/return type has no ABI-honest C
mapping (a pointer/string/struct/container the first-cut emitter refuses
rather than mis-marshal). Mirrors `FfiReconcileError`
- [FfiEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiEntry.html)
- [FfiManifest](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiManifest.html)
- [FfiReconcile](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiReconcileError.html)- Error
- PMAT-894 (Sprint-2 Tier 2): a cross-language FFI boundary could not be paired
with a defining module during `FfiManifest::reconcile``C-FFI-CPYTHON-EXT`(the contract’s`manifest_completeness`equation): in a hybrid transpile EVERY boundary that crosses a language line must resolve, or the hybrid build cannot be emitted.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Workspace](https://docs.rs/enum.WorkspaceEmitError.html)- Emit - Error
- PMAT-901 (Sprint-2 Day 2): emitting a buildable hybrid Cargo workspace
failed — either a filesystem error or the shim-emission gap
(`FfiEmitError`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [defining_](https://docs.rs/fn.defining_function.html)- function
- Recover the real defining `Function``FfiManifest::reconcile``to_lang`match.`reconcile`guarantees an entry exists only when the symbol is defined, so a miss here is an internal invariant violation (surfaced as an unsupported boundary by the caller). The defining function for a reconciled boundary: the`Item::Function`named`entry.symbol`in the module whose`source_lang`is`entry.to_lang`. Public so the`--verify`flow (PMAT-902) can read the C callee’s param/return types to build the CPython-side ctypes ABI binding for the differential reference.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_boundary_to_langs.html)- boundary_ - to_ - langs
- PMAT-898 (Sprint-2 Tier 2): resolve each module’s FFI-boundary `to_lang`from the full dispatched module set. A single-file frontend can’t see its siblings, so`depyler-frontend::detect_ffi_boundaries`records a PROVISIONAL`to_lang`(C, the canonical CPython-extension shape) for every relative import. With the whole`Vec<Module>`in hand (the`xpile hybrid`CLI), rewrite each boundary’s`to_lang`to the`source_lang`of whichever sibling module actually DEFINES the symbol. Consequences once`reconcile`runs:
- [retype_](https://docs.rs/fn.retype_float_ffi_sites.html)- float_ - ffi_ - sites
- PMAT-931 (HUNT correctness — the PMAT-930 `c_double`two-arg divergence): after reconciliation, re-type the FFI call sites of every reconciled symbol whose`to_lang`definition returns`Type::F64`so the float-repr path is selected in the calling (Python) module.

# xpile_backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-backend/0.1.615/xpile_backend/

## Expand description

Backend trait — code-lane emission abstraction.

Every target language in xpile (Rust, Ruchy, PTX, WGSL, SPIR-V, Lean)
provides one type implementing [ Backend](https://docs.rs/trait.Backend.html). The trait is intentionally
narrow: take meta-HIR and a config, return an

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`Sibling of `xpile-frontend::Frontend`. Architectural invariants
codified in `contracts/xpile-backend-trait-v1.yaml`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- Emitted artifact — primary source/IR text plus sidecar files plus the structural citation chain to Layer-5 compile contracts.
- [Backend](https://docs.rs/struct.BackendConfig.html)- Config
- Configuration passed to `Backend::lower`
- [Emitted](https://docs.rs/struct.EmittedText.html)- Text
- Plain text emitted by a single `TargetEmitter``Artifact``QuorumStatus`(that’s chosen by the wrapper).
- [Multi](https://docs.rs/struct.MultiEmitterBackend.html)- Emitter - Backend
- Multi-emitter backend wrapper. Composes a general emitter
(mandatory) + an optional specialist under a `QuorumPolicy``Backend``TranspileSession`.
- [ViaEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.ViaEntry.html)
- A single emitter entry from `compile_targets.via`in the YAML schema. Mirrors the structured-record form spec’d in`sub/layer5-multi-emitter-quorum.md`§“Contract YAML schema extension”.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Backend](https://docs.rs/enum.BackendError.html)- Error
- [Diff](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffExecResult.html)- Exec - Result
- Result of a `DiffExec`quorum policy execution. Two PTX (or WGSL/ SPIR-V) programs were run on test inputs; the engine compared their numerical outputs.
- [Emitter](https://docs.rs/enum.EmitterRole.html)- Role
- Role of a backend emitter within a multi-emitter quorum.
- [HwProfile](https://docs.rs/enum.HwProfile.html)
- Hardware profile for targets whose emission depends on hardware
capabilities (PTX `compute_capability`, WGSL feature set, SPIR-V version).
- [Profile](https://docs.rs/enum.Profile.html)
- Lowering profile — the two-mHIR asymmetric decision for Rust↔Ruchy.
- [Quorum](https://docs.rs/enum.QuorumPolicy.html)- Policy
- Policy for combining outputs when both General and Specialist
emitters fire on the same input. Configured per Layer-5 contract
via `compile_targets.quorum_policy`in the YAML.
- [Quorum](https://docs.rs/enum.QuorumStatus.html)- Status
- Status of a multi-emitter quorum vote, attached to an `Artifact`
- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.Target.html)
- Target language a backend can emit.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Backend](https://docs.rs/trait.Backend.html)
- Code-lane emission trait. See `docs/specifications/sub/backend-trait.md`.
- [Diff](https://docs.rs/trait.DiffExecEngine.html)- Exec - Engine
- PMAT-486 (§30 Track 4): engine that executes two emitted programs on contract-fixture inputs and numerically compares the outputs within a tolerance — the Runtime-stratum half of the §29 quorum. The trait + hook land here (free CI); the real CUDA / Vulkan implementations (PMAT-488 / PMAT-490) run out-of-band on self-hosted GPU runners.
- [Target](https://docs.rs/trait.TargetEmitter.html)- Emitter
- Single-emitter trait — sub-trait of a multi-emitter backend.
One `TargetEmitter``MultiEmitterBackend`

# xpile_meta_hir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-meta-hir/0.1.615/xpile_meta_hir/

## Expand description

Canonical meta-HIR.

Every frontend in xpile lowers its language-specific AST to this
shared, intentionally minimal IR. The federated approach (see
`docs/specifications/xpile-architecture-v1.md`) means we start
lossy and grow as hybrid-transpile cases demand.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)
- [FfiBoundary](https://docs.rs/struct.FfiBoundary.html)
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html)
- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html)
- [Param](https://docs.rs/struct.Param.html)
- [SortKey](https://docs.rs/struct.SortKey.html)
- PMAT-502z (Tranche 2): a `sorted(xs, key=lambda p: e)`sort key — the lambda’s single parameter name plus its (already-lowered) body. The body is lowered with`param`left unbound (an`Ident`), so it works for bodies that don’t need the param’s precise static type (arithmetic,`len(p)`, most builtins); the backend emits`let <param> = __k.clone();`to bind it by value at runtime. Str-method keys (`p.upper()`) are deferred.
- [TryHandler](https://docs.rs/struct.TryHandler.html)
- PMAT-1059: one `except`clause of a multi-handler statement-form`Stmt::TryCatch``as <name>`message binding, and handler statement block.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)
- [Dict](https://docs.rs/enum.DictViewKind.html)- View - Kind
- PMAT-502v (Tranche 2): dict view methods carried by `Expr::DictView`
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)
- [FloatOp](https://docs.rs/enum.FloatOp.html)
- PMAT-477 (R8): float arithmetic operators. Carried by
`Expr::FloatBinOp``Add`/`Sub`/`Mul`/`Div`emit plain infix (`f64`saturates, no`checked_*`);`Div`is IEEE-754 true division. PMAT-502br:`FloorDiv`/`Mod`emit Python-correct*floor*semantics (`(a / b).floor()`and`a - b * (a / b).floor()`), which differ from Rust’s truncating`/`int-div and sign-of-dividend`%`— so they are NOT plain infix.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)
- [List](https://docs.rs/enum.ListMutateOp.html)- Mutate - Op
- PMAT-502ap (Tranche 2): no-argument in-place list mutators carried by
`Stmt::ListMutate``Vec`method; all return`None`in Python (so they only appear as expression statements).
- [List](https://docs.rs/enum.ListQueryOp.html)- Query - Op
- PMAT-502u (Tranche 2): list query methods carried by `Expr::ListQuery``Int`;`Index`panics on a missing element (Python`ValueError`).
- [Loop](https://docs.rs/enum.LoopKind.html)- Kind
- POSIX shell loop dialects. PMAT-048 / XPILE-BASHRS-MERGER-001
Layer B. Each variant carries the loop’s control predicate /
item list; the body lives in `Stmt::ShellLoop::body`.
- [NumBuiltin](https://docs.rs/enum.NumBuiltinOp.html)- Op
- PMAT-498 (Tranche 2): scalar numeric builtins carried by
`Expr::NumBuiltin``Abs`takes 1 arg;`Min`/`Max`are variadic (`>= 2`args, PMAT-502cz) and chain`.min`/`.max`over the tail.
- [Pair](https://docs.rs/enum.PairIterKind.html)- Iter - Kind
- PMAT-495 (sprint): the iterator adapter for a `Stmt::ForEachPair`
- [Quoting](https://docs.rs/enum.QuotingStrategy.html)- Strategy
- Per-arg shell quoting choice. Carried by `Expr::QuotedString`so the bashrs-backend renders each arg in the strategy the source indicated. v0.1.0’s bashrs-frontend doesn’t have a real quoting-aware parser yet — it produces`Expr::LitStr`for every arg, and`QuotingStrategy::None`is implicit there. The full strategy set is wired so the v0.2.0 source fold’s real bashrs parser can plug in without IR churn.
- [Radix](https://docs.rs/enum.Radix.html)
- PMAT-502cv: the radix for `hex`/`oct`/`bin`(`Expr::IntRadixStr`).
- [SetOp](https://docs.rs/enum.SetOp.html)
- PMAT-502g (Tranche 2): set-algebra operators carried by `Expr::SetOp``HashSet`method that returns an iterator of borrows, materialized via`.cloned().collect()`into a new owned`HashSet`.
- [SetPred](https://docs.rs/enum.SetPredOp.html)- Op
- PMAT-502ep (Tranche 2): set predicates carried by `Expr::SetPred``bool`. Each maps to a`HashSet`query method; the proper variants additionally require the sets to differ.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/enum.SourceLang.html)- Lang
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)
- [StrMethod](https://docs.rs/enum.StrMethodOp.html)- Op
- PMAT-492 (sprint): no-argument Python string transform methods,
carried by `Expr::StrMethod`
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)
- MVP type lattice. Will grow as frontends demand it. Keep semantically
minimal; map source-language type idiosyncrasies (Python int bigint
promotion, C signed/unsigned, etc.) at the frontend boundary.
PMAT-455 — `Type`is no longer`Copy`because`Type::List(Box<Type>)`is heap-allocated. Callers that previously relied on`*ty`to dereference / copy now use`.clone()`(cheap — most Type values are leaf variants or 1-deep boxes).
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [collect_](https://docs.rs/fn.collect_block_idents.html)- block_ - idents
- PMAT-736 (HUNT-V11 V11-6): collect every identifier-position name reachable
from `block`into`acc`— both value references (`Expr::Ident`, a`Call`callee) and receiver names (`xs.append(...)`’s`xs`,`d[k] = v`’s`d`, …), plus binding names (a`let`, a loop var). It is the read-only mirror of the`escape_*`walker above: every`escape_name(x)`there becomes`acc.insert(x)`here, so the two stay structurally identical (both are compiler-checked exhaustive over`Stmt`/`Expr`). Used by the frontend’s nested-function lowering to decide whether a nested`def`is self-recursive and whether it captures an enclosing local — over-collection (a binding name, a lambda param) is harmless there, since the caller only intersects the result with the enclosing scope.
- [escape_](https://docs.rs/fn.escape_rust_reserved_idents.html)- rust_ - reserved_ - idents
- PMAT-573: rewrite every identifier in `module`that collides with a Rust keyword to its raw form`r#kw`, so Python locals/params/functions named`type`/`match`/`loop`/… emit valid Rust (and Ruchy). The Rust-family backends call this on a*cloned*module before emission. Struct/enum type names, struct field names, and method names are left unescaped (a keyword-named class/field/method is a separate, rarer fidelity gap).
- [retype_](https://docs.rs/fn.retype_ffi_float_call_sites.html)- ffi_ - float_ - call_ - sites
- Re-type the call sites of `float_ffi`FFI symbols in`module`to F64 so the float-repr path (print`.0`,`let: f64`, float return) is selected. See the PMAT-931 block above. No-op when`float_ffi`is empty.

# xpile_oracle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-oracle/0.1.615/xpile_oracle/

## Expand description

Oracle trait.

An [ Oracle](https://docs.rs/trait.Oracle.html) runs the

*original*source (CPython, gcc-compiled C, the ruchy interpreter) on an input fixture, captures outputs, and lets the agent compare them against transpiled Rust output. This is the semantic gate the agent must pass to exit successfully.

The pattern is borrowed from alchemize: extract reference values
*before* the agent runs, then validate against them.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [CExtension](https://docs.rs/struct.CExtensionOracle.html)- Oracle
- The `cc`-compiled C reference oracle for a single`int(int)`symbol.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/struct.CapturedOutputs.html)- Outputs
- [Ctypes](https://docs.rs/struct.CtypesBinding.html)- Binding
- One boundary symbol’s `ctypes`ABI for the CPython hybrid reference.`argtypes`/`restype`are bare`ctypes`type names (e.g.`"c_int"`,`"c_double"`);`restype == None`binds a`void`callee (`restype = None`).
- [Fixture](https://docs.rs/struct.Fixture.html)
- [Python](https://docs.rs/struct.PythonOracle.html)- Oracle
- The CPython reference oracle. Captures the stdout of running a Python module’s
`main()`under the system`python3`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_cpython_hybrid_ref.html)- cpython_ - hybrid_ - ref
- Capture the CPython reference for a hybrid Python+C module: `cc`-compile`c_sources`into a shared object, bind each`CtypesBinding`symbol via`ctypes`, strip the C-extension relative import from`py_source`, and run its`main()`under`python3`, returning stdout (trailing newline trimmed). Requires`cc`+`python3`; callers should graceful-skip when either is absent (mirror`PythonOracle::available``CExtensionOracle::available`
- [diff_](https://docs.rs/fn.diff_stdout.html)- stdout
- Compare two captured stdout strings (CPython reference vs transpiled-Rust).
Returns `ComparisonResult::Match``Divergence`pinning the first differing line for a readable failure message.

# xpile_llm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-llm/0.1.615/xpile_llm/

## Expand description

LLM invocation + content-addressed cache.

Cache key is `sha256(source_bytes || xpile_version || model_id || skills_hash)`.
On cache hit, returns the exact bytes stored — byte-identical across
runs and machines. This is what makes the stochastic agent loop
reproducible at the artifact level.

See `contracts/xpile-determinism-v1.yaml` (TODO).

# dynstaller 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/dynstaller/0.1.0

# dynstaller

## Installing Windows Sandbox

Instructions are provided by Microsoft [here](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-isolation/windows-sandbox/windows-sandbox-install). Otherwise, open a PowerShell terminal as an administrator and run the following command:

```
Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -FeatureName "Containers-DisposableClientVM" -All -Online
```
## Running Windows Sandbox

To run a .wsb (Windows Sandbox configuration file), you can double-click the file in File Explorer or pass it via command line:

```
"C:\Windows\System32\WindowsSandbox.exe" "C:\path\to\your\file.wsb"
```
## Support

Full user guides for dynstaller are available [online](https://dynstaller.readthedocs.io)
and in the [docs](https://docs.rs/docs) directory.

For questions or support, please create a new discussion on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/LLNL/dynstaller/discussions/categories/q-a),
or [open an issue](https://github.com/LLNL/dynstaller/issues/new/choose) for bug reports and feature requests.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome. Bug fixes or minor changes are preferred via a
pull request to the [dynstaller GitHub repository](https://github.com/LLNL/dynstaller).
For more information on contributing see the [CONTRIBUTING](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md) file.

## License

dynstaller is released under the MIT license. See the [LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE)
and [NOTICE](https://docs.rs/NOTICE) files for details. All new contributions must be made
under this license.

# openlineage_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openlineage-client/0.0.4/openlineage_client/

## Expand description

Transport-agnostic [OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io) event model and emit client.

This crate owns the emission side of OpenLineage: the [ RunEvent](https://docs.rs/event/struct.RunEvent.html) model and
its typed facets, a pluggable

[sink, and a non-blocking](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html)

`Transport`[that hands events to a background drain task. It has](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html)

`OpenLineageClient`**no DataFusion (or any engine) dependency**— engine integrations such as

[build on top of it, and so can any other emitter.](https://docs.rs/datafusion-openlineage)

`datafusion-openlineage`[§](https://docs.rs#the-transport-seam)The transport seam

How events are published is deliberately unspecified. The [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) trait
is the only seam: an implementation might POST to a spec-compliant OpenLineage
REST endpoint, publish to a Kafka topic, or do anything else. The crate ships

[,](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.NoopTransport.html)

`NoopTransport`[, and — behind the](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.ConsoleTransport.html)

`ConsoleTransport``http` feature —
[, which posts to an (optionally authenticated) HTTP endpoint via](https://docs.rs/cloud/struct.CloudClientTransport.html)

`CloudClientTransport``olai-http`. To target something else, implement [.](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html)

`Transport`[§](https://docs.rs#non-blocking-emission)Non-blocking emission

[ OpenLineageClient::emit](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html#method.emit) never blocks and never applies back-pressure: it
hands the event to a bounded channel drained by a background task. If the
queue is full the event is dropped with a warning — lineage must never slow or
break the host workload. Call

[before exit to drain queued events and flush the transport.](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html#method.shutdown)

`OpenLineageClient::shutdown`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::sync::Arc;
use openlineage_client::{ConsoleTransport, OpenLineageClient};
let client = OpenLineageClient::new(Arc::new(ConsoleTransport));
client.emit(event);          // non-blocking
client.shutdown().await;     // drain + flush before exit
```
[§](https://docs.rs#environment)Environment

[ OpenLineageClient::from_env](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html#method.from_env) and

[read the standard OpenLineage environment variables, so an integration can wire itself up from the environment the rest of the ecosystem already uses:](https://docs.rs/config/struct.OpenLineageConfig.html#method.from_env)

`OpenLineageConfig::from_env`| Variable | Read by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `OPENLINEAGE_URL` | `OpenLineageClient::from_env` | Base URL of the endpoint (unset → no-op client) |
| `OPENLINEAGE_ENDPOINT` | `OpenLineageClient::from_env` | Path appended to the URL (default `/api/v1/lineage`) |
| `OPENLINEAGE_API_KEY` | `OpenLineageClient::from_env` | Bearer token, if set |
| `OPENLINEAGE_NAMESPACE` | `OpenLineageConfig::from_env` | Default job namespace |
| `OPENLINEAGE_TIMEOUT_MS` | `OpenLineageConfig::from_env` | Per-request transport timeout |
| `OPENLINEAGE_PARENT_ID`/`OPENLINEAGE_PARENT_*` | `LineageContext::from_env` | Parent run facet |

# headwaters_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/headwaters-client/0.0.4/headwaters_client/

## Expand description

An async Rust client for the [Headwaters](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/headwaters)
read API.

[ HeadwatersClient](https://docs.rs/struct.HeadwatersClient.html) wraps the generated ConnectRPC client with one method
per read RPC, returning owned response messages. Build one from a base URL:

```
use headwaters_client::HeadwatersClient;
let client = HeadwatersClient::connect("http://localhost:8091")?;
// Browse, then walk the lineage graph.
let dataset = client.get_dataset("analytics", "orders").await?;
let node = headwaters_client::dataset_node_id("analytics", "orders");
let graph = client.get_lineage(&node, 2).await?;
println!("{} reachable nodes", graph.graph.len());
```
The open-ended `facets` / `data` / `fields` / `events` fields on the response
messages are `google.protobuf.Struct`; [ struct_to_json](https://docs.rs/types/fn.struct_to_json.html) turns one into a

[.](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.150/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html)

`serde_json::Value`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use nodeid::`- [dataset_field_node_id](https://docs.rs/nodeid/fn.dataset_field_node_id.html);
- `pub use nodeid::`- [dataset_node_id](https://docs.rs/nodeid/fn.dataset_node_id.html);
- `pub use nodeid::`- [job_node_id](https://docs.rs/nodeid/fn.job_node_id.html);
- `pub use`- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Build the `nodeId`strings the lineage graph addresses nodes by.

# fugazi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fugazi/0.7.0/fugazi/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fugazi)Fugazi

A library of technical-analysis (TA) building blocks designed around
*incremental* computation. Every primitive owns its internal state and is
advanced one sample at a time through `update()`, carrying just enough
intermediate state to produce the next output in O(1) (or close to it).
This makes the same code usable for live streaming and batch backtesting.

The crate has three composable layers:

- `Indicator`- *sources*. Each incrementally produces a- `Real`- **owns its own input source**, so composition is just nesting constructors:- `Ema::new(Current::close(), 20)`is the EMA-20 of the close,- `Ema::new(Sma::new(src, 10), 20)`an EMA of an SMA. Outputs are exposed as public fields refreshed every- `Indicator::update`- `value`. Leaf sources (- `Value`- `Identity`- `Current::*`for candle fields) terminate the chain. Bar indicators (- `Atr`- `Adx`- `Candle`
- `Signal`- *composable*booleans, which are simply- `Indicator`- `Output`is- `bool`. Comparison signals are built from two sources, so a condition like “RSI over 70” is a single object; combine them further with the- `BoolIndicatorExt`- `and`/- `or`/- `xor`/- `not`/- `changed`).- `Signal`itself names a- `bool`indicator fed a- `Candle`- `Box<dyn Signal>`.
- `Strategy`- *decision*layer. Unlike the pure layers below it, a strategy- *acts*, in two steps:- `update`- `trade`- `Wallet`- `wallet.set`/- `close`, with a- `Side`- `Size`- `Wallet::update`- `Reference`- `Units`- `Wallet`- *trait*, so the same strategy runs against a- `PaperWallet`

```
use fugazi::prelude::*;
use fugazi::indicators::{Identity, Rsi};
// "RSI(14) over 70" as a single bool-valued indicator over a raw price
// stream. Indicators own their source, so `Identity` feeds it into the RSI.
let mut overbought = Rsi::new(Identity::new(), 14).above(70.0);
for price in [44.0, 44.3, 44.1, 43.6, 44.3, 44.8, 45.1, 45.6] {
    overbought.update(price);
}
let _ = overbought.is_true();
```

# mdcast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mdcast/0.1.0/mdcast/

## Expand description

mdcast — Markdown → DOCX/PDF/PPTX/HTML with per-page layout templates.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [assets](https://docs.rs/assets/index.html)
- Asset resolution. Backends fetch templates, reference docs, images, etc.
through this trait — never `std::fs`. The default impl bakes the built-in catalog in via`rust-embed`; consumers wrap or replace it.
- [backends](https://docs.rs/backends/index.html)
- Backend registry. Per-target dispatch sits in `Registry::render`; backends themselves are feature-gated so a consumer can build with only what they need.
- [brand](https://docs.rs/brand/index.html)
- Brand specification: single source of truth for palette, fonts, margins, and the auto-layout rules. v1 only models what the page-layout system needs; richer projection (palette → typst/CSS/reference docs) lands in Phase 4.
- [images](https://docs.rs/images/index.html)
- Resolve markdown image references through the `AssetProvider`.
- [pages](https://docs.rs/pages/index.html)
- Page-aware IR for the doc body. Stage 1 (splitter) parses the surface
syntaxes into `RawPage`s; stage 2 (auto) assigns a`class`to produce`Page`s ready for backends.
- [preprocessor](https://docs.rs/preprocessor/index.html)
- User-pluggable markdown preprocessor.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- What a backend produced. Backends may write multiple files (e.g. HTML + assets); the primary artifact is the one a caller should hand back to the user.
- [Asset](https://docs.rs/struct.AssetRef.html)- Ref
- Reference to an external asset that the renderer should resolve via the
`AssetProvider`(e.g. an SVG rendered from a Mermaid pre-step).
- [Brand](https://docs.rs/struct.BrandHandle.html)- Handle
- Opaque handle into a `BrandSpec`so backends don’t carry the whole spec around.
- [DocMeta](https://docs.rs/struct.DocMeta.html)
- Document-level metadata extracted from frontmatter / config.
- [Render](https://docs.rs/struct.RenderRequest.html)- Request
- Per-render input passed to every backend. Holds the doc, the asset provider, and the destination path. Borrowed so the renderer never owns runtime state.
- [Resolved](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolvedDoc.html)- Doc
- The pipeline currency. OUR type — never pandoc’s AST.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.Target.html)
- Output target. One backend per variant.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Backend](https://docs.rs/trait.Backend.html)
- Every output format is one impl. Pandoc is just one kind of guest. Async because resolving templates and engine subprocesses are inherently async.
